intent.title: Startups Don't Start Themselves
intent.markdown:
Here's the mental model that changes everything: a startup is not a seed you plant and water. At the very beginning it has no momentum of its own. The founders are the engine that gets it moving — by sheer manual force — until it can finally run on its own.

Nothing about the early days is automatic. The growth you eventually want to be self-sustaining has to first be created by hand.

> Like **hand-cranking an old car engine** — you spin it by force until the motor catches and runs on its own. No crank, no ride.

Right panel label: "MANUAL FORCE → SELF-SUSTAINING"; dial reads "0 REVS" with status "STALLED — NO MOTION" and a "TURN THE CRANK" button

The causal link (manual effort leading to self-running growth) is clearly there.

slides.title: The First Unscalable Move: Recruit Users by Hand

intent.title: The First Unscalable Move: Recruit Users by Hand
intent.markdown:
If founders must manually push, what does that actually look like? Most often, it's getting users **one at a time, in person**.

- You don't wait for users to discover you — you go to them.
- Stripe's founders would walk people through setup on the spot ('the Collison installation').
- Airbnb's founders went door-to-door in New York to sign up hosts.

This feels backwards. It looks like the opposite of building a scalable business. That's exactly why it works — and why almost no one does it.

claim_at_rest.read_claim: Founders should get their first users by personally recruiting them one at a time, in person, the way Stripe and Airbnb did. It doesn't scale, and that is exactly why it works.

intent.title: Why Founders Resist
intent.markdown:
If recruiting users by hand works so well, why don't founders do it? The resistance is the heart of the story.

- **Temperament:** many founders are shy hackers who'd rather build than talk to strangers. Cranking the engine feels uncomfortable and exhausting.
- **The numbers look pathetic:** signing up users one by one yields tiny absolute totals. It feels like it can't possibly matter.

Both instincts are traps. The discomfort and the small numbers are not signs you're doing it wrong — they're the normal texture of the earliest days.

claim_at_rest.reasoning: The reader got the full assertion. They named both reasons founders resist: the discomfort and the tiny-looking numbers. They also got the main point, that both are traps and are the normal texture of the early days, not signs of doing it wrong. The only thing missing is the reason behind the discomfort (many founders are shy hackers who would rather build), which is a small detail. The reader also says founders "stop" recruiting, where the slide says they don't do it, but the claim is the same.

intent.title: The Math Founders Underestimate
intent.markdown:
Those tiny numbers feel like failure because founders judge them as a snapshot instead of a rate. The thing that matters isn't *how many* users today — it's *how fast the number compounds*.

At 10% growth per week, 100 users becomes millions within about two years. The early total is supposed to look small; the slope is what you're building.

> Like **a single fold of paper** — one fold seems trivial, but fold it 42 times and it would reach the moon. Compounding hides enormous outcomes inside unimpressive beginnings.

Chart point labels "100", "1.2k", "14k", "169k", "2.0M" along a curve that stays flat and then shoots up near "2 YR"
"Linear view: the early slope looks like nothing — yet the count keeps doubling." (caption under chart)
"The early total is supposed to look small. The slope is the thing you're actually building." (left column)
"Compound growth · 10% per week" (eyebrow, top)

intent.title: Fragile Things Get Misjudged
intent.markdown:
Because early numbers are tiny, outsiders (and founders themselves) judge a startup by the standards of established companies — and conclude it's a toy. But nearly every startup is extremely fragile at the start. That fragility is normal, not fatal.

The right question isn't 'how big is this now?' It's 'how big could this get if the founders did the right things?'

> Like **judging an oak by the acorn** — measured as it is today, it looks like nothing. Measured by what it could become, it's a forest.

AN ACORN.

intent.title: Delight: Be Insanely Great, Not Just Build It
intent.markdown:
Manual effort isn't only about acquiring users — it's about overwhelming the ones you have. Take extraordinary, unscalable measures to delight them: hand-written notes, personal attention, a level of care big companies literally cannot afford to give.

Notice the reframe: aim for an insanely great *experience*, not necessarily an insanely great *product*. Attentiveness can cover for software that's still early, buggy, and incomplete — and that close contact is also your best feedback loop for making the product genuinely good.

> Like **a tiny family restaurant** where the owner remembers your name — the food may be simple, but the care makes it unforgettable in a way no chain can match.

claim_at_rest.read_claim: A startup with a rough product can still give users an insanely great experience, beating a big company's polished product, by putting in personal care that doesn't scale and that big companies can't afford.
read_evidence: Aim for an insanely great experience — not necessarily a great product.
PERCEIVED EXPERIENCE = PRODUCT + CARE
BIG COMPANY ... POLISHED PRODUCT · ZERO CARE
YOU (STARTUP) ... ROUGH PRODUCT | HAND-WRITTEN NOTES · PERSONAL ATTENTION (bar extends past the 'INSANELY GREAT' dashed line)
92/100 INSANELY GREAT
THE MOVE TAKE EXTRAORDINARY, UNSCALABLE MEASURES TO OVERWHELM THE USERS YOU ALREADY HAVE

claim_at_rest.reasoning: The reader got the main claim: unscalable personal care can make up for a rough early product and produce an insanely great experience that big companies can't afford to give. That covers the reframe from product to experience and the reason it works. What's missing is the secondary point that this close contact is also the best feedback loop for making the product genuinely good. The reader also leaves out that the manual effort is aimed at existing users rather than at acquiring new ones, though the slide's 'The Move' line does say this.

With the sentences covered, a viewer can still see that a rough product plus a large block of care reaches as far as, or past, a polished product with no care. The slider makes this work: dragging it lengthens the care segment, and the experience total updates. The secondary points (care is cheap for startups, close contact is a feedback loop) appear only in the text, so this is a 3 rather than a 4. The bars are also mostly a static comparison, and the score readout is just a number.

'you can pour in care for free' — the source repeatedly calls these efforts 'laborious' and 'extraordinary measures'. Its point is that founders have 'nothing to lose', not that care costs nothing. Calling it free goes against the essay's main theme of unscalable effort.

'You can't move product fast' — the source doesn't say this. In the Meraki section it says founders 'can tweak the design faster when you're the factory', and it encourages shipping early and iterating.

'POLISHED PRODUCT · ZERO CARE' — 'zero care' overstates the source. The source only says big companies can't give individual hand-written attention, and that customer-service standards are 'set by the big companies'.

But several framing lines in the side panel and caption shift the source's meaning. They turn the big company's inability into indifference ('can't be bothered'), call care 'free' when the essay stresses it is laborious, and add an unsupported claim that startups can't move product fast. Each is small on its own, but together they are a material distortion of the reasoning behind 'why the gap is yours'.

slides.title: The Idea Is a Vector, Not a Point

intent.title: The Idea Is a Vector, Not a Point
intent.markdown:
Pulling it all together: a startup idea isn't just *what you'll build*. It's a vector with two parts — **what you'll build** plus **the unscalable things you'll do to get it started**.

- Hardware founders can assemble the first units by hand ('pull a Meraki').
- B2B founders can act as consultants, building for a single user, or do tasks manually before automating them.
- Beware the strategies that omit real effort — the Big Launch, the big-company partnership. Any plan that lets you skip the cranking is suspect.

Ideally, those early unscalable habits don't disappear once you scale — they become permanent DNA: a company that stays unusually attentive because that's how it learned to live.

items.q: What does the car-engine crank metaphor say about how startups take off?
items.ref: Startups don't usually take off on their own. The founders have to push them through a separate, laborious start-up phase, like hand-cranking an engine, and after that the engine keeps running by itself.
items.answer: A startup has no momentum of its own. The founders have to turn it over by hand, the way you'd hand-crank an old car engine, until the motor catches and runs by itself. Self-sustaining growth has to be created at first by sheer manual force.
items.why: Gets the key idea: founders push the startup through a manual start-up phase, like hand-cranking an engine, until it runs by itself.

items.q: Why does the essay argue that recruiting users one by one is worth it even though the numbers seem tiny at first?
items.ref: Because of compound growth. If you keep up a steady weekly growth rate like 10%, small absolute gains build into huge numbers (about 14,000 users after one year and 2 million after two), so manual recruiting can get you to scale.
items.answer: Founders should judge the number as a rate, not a snapshot. Compound growth, such as 10% a week, turns 100 users into about 2.0M in two years, so the early total is supposed to look small and the slope is what you're really building.
items.why: Names compound growth at about 10% a week and the roughly 2M users after two years, so small manual gains build to scale.

items.q: What mistake do inexperienced founders and investors make when they judge early startups, and what question should they ask instead?
items.ref: They judge fragile, larval startups by the standards of established companies and dismiss them. Instead they should ask how big the company could get if the founders did the right things.
items.answer: They judge a fragile early startup by the yardstick of established companies, asking 'How big is this now?', and call it a toy. They should ask instead 'How big could this get if the founders did the right things?'
items.why: Gives both the mistake (judging fragile startups by established-company standards) and the right question to ask instead.

items.q: How can a small startup give better customer service than a big company, and why do founders often fail to see this?
items.ref: Being small lets founders give personal attention that big companies can't, like hand-written thank-you notes. Founders miss this because their standards for service were set by the big companies they've been customers of, and because engineers aren't trained in customer service.
items.answer: Big companies max out the product but can't afford personal care, while a startup can pour in care for free, like hand-written notes and personal attention, to beat the big player's polished product. The deck does not say why founders often fail to see this.
items.why: Explains how being small allows personal care, but leaves out why founders miss it (standards set by big companies, engineers untrained in service).

items.q: In a startup's early months, how does the meaning of 'insanely great' shift, and why does over-engaging with users improve the product?
items.ref: What should be insanely great is the experience of being a user, not the product, so attentiveness can make up for a buggy, incomplete product. Engaging directly with early users also gives the best feedback, which drives the iteration that makes the product good.
items.answer: The deck says to aim for an insanely great experience rather than necessarily a great product, with care making up for an early, buggy, incomplete product. It also says the same close contact with users is your sharpest feedback loop.
items.why: Covers both points: the user's experience is what should be great, with care making up for a buggy product, and close contact gives the best feedback.

items.q: Why might a startup deliberately start in a narrow market, as Facebook did with Harvard?
items.ref: Like keeping a fire contained so it gets hot, a narrow market lets you reach critical mass quickly because the users feel the product is really for them. You can then expand from there.
items.answer: Hand-cranking only works when effort is concentrated, and spreading a fixed effort across many markets leaves every one below the point where it catches (critical mass). Facebook launched at Harvard only because it was a world small enough to fully win before moving on, like getting kindling blazing before adding big logs.
items.why: Gets the main ideas of concentrated effort, reaching critical mass, a contained fire and expanding afterward, but misses that users feel the product is really for them.

items.q: What benefits come from doing things manually that you plan to automate later, or from building hardware yourself, as Meraki and Pebble did?
items.ref: It lets you launch faster and avoid obstacles like large minimum factory orders. You also learn exactly what to build or automate, and in hardware you can tweak the design faster, because you've done the work yourself.
items.answer: The deck only says to assemble the first hardware units yourself ('pull a Meraki'), which gives the idea its unscalable component. Over time the unscalable work becomes permanent DNA, a company that stays unusually attentive; Pebble and manual-then-automate are not covered.
items.why: Misses the key benefits of launching faster, avoiding minimum factory orders, and learning what to build, and says Pebble isn't covered.

items.q: Why does the essay reject the 'Big Launch' and big-company partnerships, and what does it mean to think of startup ideas as vectors rather than scalars?
items.ref: Startups are like powered aircraft, not projectiles: success depends on sustained effort and on how happy you make your first users, not on initial velocity, and strategies that skip the effort are suspect.
